description: We are Cheikh and Mouhamed, co-founders of SIKKI SAKKA Intelligence, a Decision Intelligence studio based in Senegal. Our team combines data science, quantitative modeling, software engineering, and decision analysis. Through S² FieldShift, we aim to help farmers explore resilient crop rotations using NASA Earth observations, agronomic evidence, and robust decision methods under climate uncertainty.
summary:
Farmers must choose what to plant before climate uncertainty disappears. But what happens when two NASA rainfall products tell different stories?

S² FieldShift, developed by SIKKI SAKKA Intelligence for Senegal's groundnut basin, is an interactive prototype connecting Earth observations to transparent crop-planning decisions.

For June–September 2024 in Kaolack, NASA POWER reports 756.9 mm of rainfall, while GPM IMERG estimates 637.0 mm—a 119.9 mm difference between products, not a measured error. FieldShift makes such disagreements visible and lets users explore two-season millet, groundnut, cowpea and sorghum rotations under declared field constraints.

Its decision tools demonstrate how changing priorities can reverse an illustrative preference. Crucially, the agricultural evidence gate withholds a crop ranking when local soil, yield and rotation-effect evidence is insufficient.

FieldShift does not claim proven yield improvements. It shows how NASA data, transparent assumptions and explicit limits can support more responsible agricultural decision-making.

From Doubt to Decision.
details:
S² FieldShift — From Climate Observations to Responsible Farming Decisions

Farmers must choose what to plant before uncertainty disappears. But when satellite rainfall estimates disagree, which conclusions can they trust?

Built by SIKKI SAKKA Intelligence for Senegal's groundnut basin, S² FieldShift is an interactive prototype that connects NASA Earth observations to crop-planning decisions.

For June–September 2024 in Kaolack, NASA POWER estimates 756.9 mm of rain, versus 637.0 mm from GPM IMERG—a 119.9 mm difference between products, not a measured error. FieldShift makes that disagreement visible through daily comparisons, historical climate diagnostics and a rainfall atlas.

Users can explore two-season sequences involving millet, groundnut, cowpea and sorghum, examine declared field constraints and test how changing priorities alters illustrative preferences. Interactive reversal thresholds and minimax-regret examples explain decision sensitivity; their scores are synthetic, not agronomic predictions.

Crucially, an evidence gate withholds a crop ranking when local soil, yield or rotation-effect data are insufficient. Observations, assumptions and missing evidence remain distinct.

Built with React, TypeScript and Python, FieldShift demonstrates a practical principle: better decisions begin by knowing what the evidence can—and cannot—support.

Live: https://s2-fieldshift.pages.dev
Code: https://github.com/cabsow11/s2-fieldshift
